text: For the choirmaster: to the tune of "Do Not Destroy." A psalm of Asaph. A song.
We give you thanks, O God, we give you thanks, for your name is near; people recount your wonders.
"When I take up the appointed time, it is I who judge with fairness.

versions.text: "I choose the appointed time; I am the one who judges with equity.
versions.explanation: כִּי here is best read temporally/causally ('when/for'), setting up the second clause; the emphatic pronoun אֲנִי is well matched by 'it is I who judge.' The temporal reading also parallels the structure of the next verse and reads more smoothly aloud.

text: When the earth and all who live in it are reeling, it is I who hold its pillars firm. Selah
I say to the boastful, 'Boast no more,' and to the wicked, 'Do not lift up your horn.'
Do not lift your horn on high, or speak insolence with a stiff neck."

versions.text: Do not lift your horn against the heavens or speak with an arrogant neck."
versions.explanation: לַמָּרוֹם means 'on high, loftily' — an adverbial phrase describing haughty self-exaltation, not a target of attack. 'Against the heavens' imports an idea of assaulting God that the Hebrew does not state and shifts the image away from proud self-elevation.

versions.text: Do not lift your horn on high, or speak with an arrogant neck."
versions.explanation: In the Hebrew, עָתָק ('insolence, arrogant things') is the content of the speaking, while בְצַוָּאר ('with the neck') describes the outstretched, stiffened posture of the proud speaker. Rendering 'an arrogant neck' transfers the arrogance from the words to the neck itself; keeping insolence as the object of speech is closer to the idiom and reads just as smoothly aloud. The current wording is a defensible compression of the image.

text: For lifting up comes neither from the east nor from the west, nor from the wilderness of the mountains.

versions.text: For exaltation comes neither from the east nor from the west, nor from the desert hills.
versions.explanation: The verse has no verb in Hebrew, and הָרִים can be read either as 'mountains' or as the act of 'lifting up.' The present rendering supplies 'exaltation' and also translates הָרִים as 'hills,' effectively using the word twice. Choosing one reading (with a footnote noting the alternative, 'nor from the wilderness comes exaltation') would be clearer.

text: It is God who judges: he brings one down and lifts another up.
In the LORD's hand is a cup of foaming wine, fully mixed with spices; he pours it out, and all the wicked of the earth drink it down to the very dregs.
But as for me, I will proclaim it forever; I will sing praise to the God of Jacob.

versions.text: But I will proclaim it forever; I will sing praise to the God of Jacob.
versions.explanation: The emphatic וַאֲנִי contrasts the psalmist with the wicked of the previous verse; 'but as for me' captures this shift of speaker and reads well aloud after the judgment scene.

text: "I will cut off all the horns of the wicked, but the horns of the righteous will be lifted high."
